artifacts.notes: Uncorrected OCR of the whole volume, including front matter, Congreve's preface, Comper's editorial notes, the constituent tracts, and the glossary. Recognition errors are frequent and visible (for example 'An Moriendi' for 'Ars Moriendi', 'Justin' for 'Austin', 'Reg.' abbreviations broken across lines, and stray marginalia digits mixed into the text); it is a finding aid and a searchable witness, not a facsimile or a corrected transcription. Any wording a publication quotes from it must be read in context and reported as OCR-derived. Running heads, printed page numbers, and Comper's marginal scripture references are interleaved with the text.
artifacts.rights_basis: The underlying book was published at London and New York in 1917 without a United States copyright renewal on record, and the Internet Archive scan page states that the item carries no known copyright restriction in the United States. The mechanical scan and its uncorrected optical character recognition add no original authorship. Triptych claims no exclusive right in the source wording.

edition.publication: London: Longmans, Green, and Co., 1917, with a preface by the Rev. George Congreve, S.S.J.E.
edition.title: The Book of the Craft of Dying, and Other Early English Tracts Concerning Death, ed. Frances M. M. Comper

work.author: Frances M. M. Comper, editor; the constituent tracts are of various and partly unknown authorship
work.description: Comper's 1917 anthology of late-medieval English writings on dying, assembled from manuscripts and printed books in the British Museum and Bodleian libraries and printed in modernized spelling. The container is an edited anthology and its identity is distinct from the constituent tracts printed within it: The Craft of Dying (translated from an anonymous Latin ars moriendi, transcribed from Bodleian MS 423 and collated against Douce MS 322 and Rawlinson MS C. 894); an abridgment ascribed to William Caxton and translated from an untraced French source; a further abridgment; chapters from Suso's Horologium sapientiae, the Toure of all Toures, and Richard Rolle's Form of Living; a fragment from MS Bodley 423; and The Lamentation of the Dying Creature. Comper reports that the author of the older Latin original of The Craft of Dying is unknown, that the tract cites Gerson as an authority rather than being his work, and that the block-books of the Ars moriendi are a separate line of transmission. A locus is a page of the 1917 printing, optionally a page range.
work.title: The Book of the Craft of Dying, and Other Early English Tracts Concerning Death
